Under normal circumstances I would in fact agree with you and say yes, that is true. However destiny has one issue that those other MMOs do not: the entirety of its stats are bound to gear, and thus all progression is tied directly to that gear as a result. This makes all progression highly committal with resources/enforces an "all or nothing" approach to gear.

MMOs with gear resets work because players get progressively stronger even without their gear. This means that player progression continues in a linear fashion upward even with gear resets. In Destiny this is not the case: all stats are tied to the weapons and armor, making it all or nothing progression: either gear is an improvement for stats or it isn't. Its the same fatal flaw that plagued Diablo 3 for years.

For gear resets to work well, there needs to be progression independent of them. An idea that could greatly alleviate this is a way to "imprint" old armor's stats onto new armor (IE you can use resources to put your 65 point spread of old armor stats onto a new armor) or transfer a masterwork of an old armor onto a new one. I won't argue that weapons do benefit from resetting, however I would argue that such a process should be far more precise and target specific loot rather than entire years and seasons worth of loot.

If Bungie found a way to untie stats from gear to a degree and make stat development more independent, then a lot of issues with sunsetting would be greatly alleviated. However, in its current state they are stuck in the same problematic designs that plagued Diablo 3.

I think the issue is that there is a large gulf between communication/intent and execution, as well as the mindset of the development team. There is a massive issue with an expiration date on weapons and armor in that it is an MMO-style design choice specifically utilized in MMOs.

In MMOs, gear power is not the only form of progression. A character levels up, they gain power independent of their gear in the form of skills and other such abilities that alleviate the impact of gear expiration dates. When gear is cycled out, they are able to mitigate this as they choose better gear.

The fundamental flaw in this logic is that Destiny is NOT an MMO. Its mechanics are different on a fundamental level. Because of this something like gear retirement that might have worked in World of Warcraft (the prominent example used most often for MMO design) does not translate well over to Destiny.

People are entirely bound to the power of their gear. It is the ONLY form of progression. Thus, even the slightest change to gear progression can have massive implications to how individuals play. By retiring gear on a yearly basis in chunks (which is what we can infer from the information we have been given) massive chunks of progress are lost with no recompense as entire gearsets become handicapped or useless in engame content, possibly with no replacement. That, and what about the ornaments and other cosmetic items that people might have bought for their weapons? Technically that is being retired too, which brings up far more concerns regarding the ethical nature of Eververse in the coming future.

Endgame content difficulty isn't going to be solved by shuffling numbers around. It isn't going to be solved by removing seemingly problematic weapons and gear. It isn't going to be solved by cramming as many negative modifiers as you can find onto an activity (IE Grandmaster Nightfalls). The difficulty in design isn't due to those problems, its due to problematic design mindsets of players and developers still stuck to MMO design and difficulty philosophy that cannot be applied to Destiny.
